topics.title: Chapter 51 — Network Programming
topics.summary: Network programming extends resource and protocol reasoning across independently scheduled peers. A successful connection does not make the peer’s input valid, and a successful send does not mean that an entire application transaction has completed. Programs must define framing, bounds, byte ordering, completion, and failure behavior explicitly. The examples use local loopback TCP only. They do not provide authentication, encryption, internet deployment, or a production security policy. The goal is to understand socket lifecycle and byte-stream handling without exposing a public service. [ R26 , R27 ]

topics.title: 51.1 Sockets
topics.summary: A socket is an endpoint managed through a descriptor. Its address family and type determine the communication model. Internet stream sockets typically use TCP, while local-domain sockets and datagram sockets provide different addressing or delivery semantics. A socket descriptor follows the same ownership rules as other descriptors: one owner closes it, borrowed uses must finish before closure, and the integer can be reused afterward. Closing a descriptor from another thread is not a universal cancellation mechanism for an in-progress operation.

topics.title: 51.2 socket
topics.summary: socket creates an endpoint with a selected family, type, and protocol. It returns a descriptor or -1 . Creation does not by itself bind a listening address or establish a connection. Set required descriptor and status flags deliberately. On Linux, creation flags can establish close-on-exec or nonblocking behavior atomically. Do not assume that a later accepted socket automatically inherits every desired flag from its listener.

topics.title: 51.3 bind
topics.summary: bind associates a socket with a local address. For an IPv4 loopback service, bind to 127.0.0.1 rather than all interfaces when external access is not required. Using port zero asks the operating system to choose an available ephemeral port. Address structures contain fields with specified byte order. Use conversion functions such as htons and htonl for network-order integer fields. Do not serialize a host-native structure by dumping its memory representation and hoping another machine interprets it identically.

topics.title: 51.4 listen
topics.summary: listen places a suitable socket into a listening state. Its backlog parameter relates to pending connection handling under the platform’s rules; it is not a complete application limit on active clients, memory, or work queues. A server still needs admission control after accepting connections. Increasing backlog does not create more worker capacity or solve resource exhaustion. It changes one stage of a larger queueing system.

topics.title: 51.5 accept
topics.summary: accept obtains a new connected socket from the listener’s pending connections. The listening socket remains available for further accepts. The returned socket, not the listener, carries the client’s byte stream. [ R43 ] A nonblocking listener can return EAGAIN when no connection is currently available, including after a readiness indication whose state changed. Configure accepted-socket flags explicitly. A service that forgets to close rejected or completed client sockets leaks descriptors over time.

topics.title: 51.6 connect
topics.summary: connect requests establishment of a connection to a peer address. Blocking and nonblocking forms have different completion handling. A nonblocking connect that reports in-progress is not yet a successful usable connection; readiness and the socket error state must be checked according to the interface. [ R44 ] Connection failure is normal: the service may not exist, policy may reject access, or the network may be unavailable. Retry policy needs limits and backoff. Repeatedly reconnecting without a budget can turn a remote failure into local resource exhaustion.

topics.title: 51.8 TCP connections
topics.summary: TCP provides an ordered reliable byte stream under its protocol, not application-message boundaries. One send can be received through several reads, and several sends can be combined in one read. A positive receive result reports bytes currently obtained, not necessarily a complete request. [ R27 , R49 , R50 ] A common framing scheme uses a fixed-width length prefix followed by exactly that many payload bytes. Decode the prefix in a defined byte order, reject lengths above a configured maximum before allocating, and treat EOF in the middle of a frame as truncation. A normal EOF between frames has a different protocol meaning from a truncated frame.

topics.title: Worked example — A bounded framed loopback exchange
topics.summary: The reusable header below owns descriptors, bounds frames to 1024 bytes, handles partial transfers and EINTR , and treats premature EOF as failure. It uses Linux’s MSG_NOSIGNAL for sends so that a broken connection becomes an error instead of terminating the process through SIGPIPE . The small socket timeouts are per-operation limits, not a complete whole-request deadline policy. Companion listing: ch51/net.hpp The driver binds only loopback, obtains the chosen port, and establishes the client connection before starting the accepting worker. This avoids leaving an accept worker waiting forever if the test’s initial connect fails. The server worker catches its own exceptions; the parent checks its result after joining. Companion listing: ch51/main.cpp The expected output is loopback frame checks passed . The protocol consists of a four-byte big-endian length and payload. The test transfers one five-byte payload, but the helpers also permit an empty frame. A complete service would need repeated-frame handling, whole-request deadlines, admission control, graceful shutdown, and a security layer appropriate to its deployment.
